Neonates of Valencia hispanica, upon hatching from eggs measuring approximately 1.6 millimeters in diameter, emerge at a very modest wet weight of about 0.0021 grams [Wwb = about 0.0021 grams]. This initial body mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the lecithotrophic prolarva, which must soon transition to active feeding. Field surveys conducted in coastal lagoons of the western Mediterranean indicate that the wet weight at puberty is roughly 0.70 grams [Wwp = roughly 0.70 grams], a threshold that defines the onset of gonadal maturation. Notably, no young-of-the-year individuals have ever been found to be reproductively active, suggesting that puberty is not attained during the first growing season. This pattern implies that the standard length at which sexual maturation is initiated is approximately 3.9 centimeters [Lp = approximately 3.9 centimeters], a size that is generally achieved only after several months of sustained growth under favorable thermal conditions.

The ultimate standard length attained by adults of this species is around 8 centimeters [Li = around 8 centimeters], a figure that represents the asymptotic size reached after the completion of the main somatic growth phase. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight associated with this maximum length is approximately 6.24 grams [Wwi = approximately 6.24 grams], which is derived from a length–weight relationship typical of small-bodied cyprinodontiform fishes. This adult mass is substantially greater than the mass at puberty, highlighting the considerable somatic investment that occurs during the sub-adult stage. In field collections from Spanish coastal marshes, individuals approaching this asymptotic size are almost invariably sexually mature and actively participating in spawning events, which underscores the strong link between size and reproductive competence in this threatened killifish.

Reproduction in Valencia hispanica is characterized by a protracted spawning season that can extend from early spring through late autumn when water temperatures remain favorable. At a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], gravid females produce eggs at a maximum annual rate of approximately 300 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 300 eggs per year], a figure that integrates both the clutch size and the frequency of spawning events. This annual output is the result of females releasing small clutches on a near-daily basis during peak reproductive windows, a strategy common among small-bodied iteroparous teleosts that maximize lifetime fecundity. The high reproductive rate at this temperature likely represents an adaptation to the unpredictable hydrological conditions of the shallow, ephemeral habitats the species occupies, where breeding opportunities may be temporally restricted.

The maximum lifespan documented for Valencia hispanica under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years], a relatively extended longevity for a fish of such modest body size. This lifespan substantially exceeds the typical age at first reproduction and allows for multiple reproductive seasons over the course of an individual's life. In the wild, actual longevity may be shorter due to predation, habitat desiccation, and seasonal fluctuations in water quality. Nonetheless, the capacity for repeated annual spawning over a five-year period contributes to the species' demographic resilience, even as natural populations face increasing pressure from habitat loss and invasive species. The metabolic costs of sustaining such a long life are presumably supported by the low basal maintenance requirements typical of small, sedentary fish.

Within the family Valenciidae, Valencia hispanica occupies a niche characterized by relatively slow life-history traits that set it apart from more fecund, shorter-lived cyprinodontiforms. The late puberty onset at 3.9 centimeters [Lp = 3.9 centimeters] standard length and the annual reproductive output of 300 eggs [Ri = annual reproductive output of 300 eggs] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] are indicative of a strategy prioritizing individual survival over high immediate fecundity. This equilibrium strategy is further reflected in a maximum lifespan of 5 years [am = 5 years], which, compared to the 1–2 year lifespans of many small killifish, allows for repeated spawning seasons and a longer reproductive window at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Conservation efforts for this endangered Mediterranean endemism must consider these life-history constraints, as the species' slow maturation and moderate fecundity render it particularly vulnerable to habitat fragmentation and prolonged environmental perturbations.
